label: Synthetic Peer
info:
A did:web identity for BDD/deployment-side simulation of an untrusted peer that passes eIDAS + challenge-response (layers 1/2) but has NO agreement credential (layer 3a, ADR-19): did:web:dcs-orce%3A1880:synthetic-peer. The backend's did:web resolution (identity.DIDWebToHostname) stops at the first ':' after the host component and never uses any path segment that follows, so this identity resolves, host-and-port-wise, to this ORCE pod itself, at the bare /.well-known/ paths (NOT /synthetic-peer/.well-known/... — that prefix is never actually requested; routing there would be dead code) — mirroring instance A's real did.json (same key, so the challenge-response signature genuinely verifies) while 404ing the agreement credential.

A second identity, did:web:dcs-orce-mismatch%3A1880 (ADR-19 AC5), shares this same pod via a second Kubernetes Service alias (service-synthetic-peer-mismatch.yaml, same selector/ports) and is told apart purely by the incoming request's Host header (msg.req.headers.host) in both GET handlers below: it serves a STATIC, offline-generated did.json and agreement credential (P-256 test keypair, ecdsa-rdfc-2019 Data Integrity proof — same proof shape federation.BuildAgreementCredential produces, just software-signed instead of HSM-signed; generated once with backend/cmd/gensyntheticmismatch, which is not part of the running service) whose termsOfUse.hash is deliberately wrong (sha256 of the embedded rules document plus one extra byte) — exercising the hash-mismatch rejection (AC5) without a second build.

A THIRD identity, did:web:dcs-orce-trusted%3A1880 (ADR-19 AC7/AC8/AC9), shares the pod the same way (service-synthetic-peer-trusted.yaml, same Host-header routing) but publishes nothing checked in: the BDD harness mints a P-256 key pair per run, self-signs an agreement credential naming the federation rules hash the instance under test currently publishes, and pushes did.json + credential to POST /synthetic-trusted/identity. It is the only synthetic peer that PASSES the agreement-credential check (layer 3a), which is what lets an inbound scenario put the policy endpoint (layer 3b) under test on its own. Its documents are generated rather than checked in because a static credential's termsOfUse.hash stops matching the running build the moment backend/internal/base/federation/rules.md changes.
